June 1889. Vincent van Gogh is living at the asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where he went of his own accord to be cared for. From his window he watches the sky before dawn. But the village you have just painted never existed: Vincent invented it, with a steeple that recalls the churches of his native Holland. The cypress, like a dark flame, links the earth to the stars. Today this is one of the most famous paintings in the world. It hangs in New York.

Summer 1889, near Saint-Rémy. Van Gogh sets up his easel in the wind, in front of the ripe wheat. He loves cypresses, which he compares to Egyptian obelisks, and dreams of painting them as no one has before. Look at the clouds: they swirl like the thick paint he lays on with his brush. He loved this landscape so much that he painted three versions. This one is in the National Gallery in London.

Arles, September 1888. Van Gogh spends three nights in this café on Place Lamartine, open at all hours, where drifters sleep. He wants, he writes to his brother Theo, to express the terrible passions of humanity with red and green. The gas lamps throb with yellow halos, the billiard table casts a huge shadow. Vincent called it one of the ugliest pictures he had done, and yet one that mattered most to him.

Spring 1890. Shut away in Saint-Rémy, Van Gogh remembers his youth in northern Europe. He paints cottages with mossy roofs, smoke curling like brushstrokes, a setting sun and a peasant walking home. His letters speak of memories of the North. A few weeks later he will leave Provence for Auvers-sur-Oise, where he paints his very last pictures.

Around 1831, in Japan. Katsushika Hokusai is over seventy when he publishes his Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. This wave is the most famous of them all. Look closely: behind the foam rising like claws, Mount Fuji looks tiny. Three fishing boats dive beneath the crest. Prussian blue, brought from Europe, was then a new colour in Japan. This print was made thousands of times, and it fascinated Monet and Van Gogh alike.

Le Havre, one morning in 1872. Claude Monet paints the harbour from his window: the orange sun shines on the water, the boats are just blue shadows. Two years later he shows it in Paris as Impression, Sunrise. A critic mocks it and calls these painters impressionists. The nickname stuck, and gave its name to a whole movement.

At Giverny, Monet has a pond dug and plants water lilies of every colour. For nearly thirty years he paints this small stretch of water at every hour, in every light: more than two hundred and fifty pictures. There is no bank and no horizon, only the sky reflected between the flowers. Late in life, even as his eyesight failed, he kept painting his water lilies.

Monet settles in Giverny in 1883, in a house surrounded by meadows and poplars. Before creating his famous water garden, he paints the countryside around him, outdoors, in a few quick sessions to catch the light of the moment. Pink trees, grass dotted with flowers: the detail doesn\'t matter, the feeling of a beautiful day does.

Paul Cézanne said he wanted to astonish Paris with an apple. In this still life nothing is quite straight: the table tilts, so does the bottle, and the edge of the cloth doesn\'t line up. It isn\'t clumsiness. Cézanne shows each object from its best angle, as if we were walking around it. Picasso and the cubists would later call him the father of us all. This painting is in Chicago.

Around 1818, in Germany. Caspar David Friedrich paints a man standing on a rock above a sea of clouds. We never see his face, and that is deliberate: we look at the landscape with him, over his shoulder. This wanderer has become the symbol of Romanticism, the movement that sought vastness and emotion in nature. The painting hangs in Hamburg.

Paris, 1872. Pierre-Auguste Renoir settles upstairs in a café facing the Pont-Neuf to paint the crowd in the sun. His brother Edmond helps in his own way: he stops passers-by to ask them the time or the way, while Renoir sketches them. Blue sky, light shadows, strollers: this is the joyful Paris of early impressionism. The painting is now in Washington.

Georges Seurat is twenty-four when he begins this painting. He works on it for two years, laying tiny touches of pure colour side by side. From a distance, our eye blends them: the technique will be called pointillism. On the island of La Grande Jatte, near Paris, Parisians stroll on a Sunday with a monkey, dogs and parasols. The huge original is in Chicago.

In 1832, Eugène Delacroix joins a diplomatic mission to Morocco. In Tangier he attends a Jewish wedding and fills his notebooks with sketches and colours. Back in Paris he paints the scene from memory: the musicians, the dancers, the white light on the walls. That journey changed his painting forever. The picture is in the Louvre.

Around 1658, in Delft, in the Netherlands. Johannes Vermeer paints a maid pouring milk in a quiet kitchen. Look at the light from the window, the little bright dots on the bread, the deep blue of the apron, made from a crushed precious stone, lapis lazuli. Nothing happens, and yet everything seems suspended. Vermeer painted very few pictures, barely forty. This one is in Amsterdam.

Iowa, 1930. Grant Wood notices a small white house with a pointed Gothic window. He imagines the people who might live there, and asks his sister Nan and his dentist to pose. People often think they are husband and wife, but the painter saw them as a father and his daughter. The pitchfork is echoed in the seams of the overalls and in the window. This painting has become one of America\'s best-known images.

Joseph Mallord William Turner, the English painter of light and storms. Here a great ship breaks apart in a raging sea, while small boats try to save the crew. Turner doesn\'t paint every wave: he paints the power of nature, with sweeping gestures and colours that run into each other. More than half a century early, he points the way to the impressionists.

Edvard Munch was walking at sunset near Oslo when, he wrote, the sky turned blood red. He felt, he said, an infinite scream passing through nature. So he painted this figure clutching its head on a bridge, under a sky in flames. Munch made several versions, in paint, pastel and print. This picture has become the symbol of modern anxiety.

Leonardo da Vinci begins this portrait around 1503, in Florence. He never parts with it: he takes it to France, where he spends his last years, and keeps retouching it. His secret is called sfumato: outlines so soft they seem to melt into shadow, especially at the corners of the mouth. That is why her smile seems to change as you look at her. Stolen in 1911 and found two years later, she now lives in the Louvre.

Not a portrait but a “tronie”, an imagined face, wearing a blue and yellow turban.
Near Argenteuil, Camille and their son Jean appear twice: at the top of the hill, then in the foreground.
Camille and Jean seen from below, against the sky: Monet paints fast to catch the passing wind.
Vincent wanted the colours alone to “rest the mind”. He painted his room in the Yellow House three times.
Painted in the garden at Saint-Rémy in his very first week there, in May 1889.
Painted in Arles in August 1888 to decorate the room of his friend Paul Gauguin.
At the end of summer, at dawn, the sun turns the mountain red. Hokusai needs only three colours.
A print from the One Hundred Views of Edo. Van Gogh loved it so much he copied it in oils in 1887.
A brand-new crossroads near the Gare Saint-Lazare, where umbrellas pass on the wet cobblestones.
One of Bruegel’s paintings of the seasons: far below, the whole village skates on the frozen ponds.
Look closely: this face is made of fruit, vegetables and ears of wheat. A cherry for the lip, a pear for the chin.
At playtime, the schoolboys hold hands and run in a line: the last one has to hang on!

Delft, in the Netherlands, around 1665. Johannes Vermeer paints a girl turning towards us, lips parted, as if we had just called her name. Nobody knows who she is: this is not a commissioned portrait but an imagined face. Her turban is painted with a precious blue made from a stone, lapis lazuli, which cost more than gold. And the pearl? Two small touches of white are enough to make it shine. The painting hangs in the Mauritshuis, in The Hague.

Summer 1873, near Argenteuil, on the banks of the Seine. Claude Monet walks with his wife Camille and their son Jean through a field of poppies. Look closely: the mother with her parasol and the child appear twice, at the top of the hill and in the foreground, as if they were walking down towards us. The flowers are just quick dabs of red. The next year, Monet showed this painting at the very first Impressionist exhibition. It is now in the Musée d’Orsay, in Paris.

Summer 1875. Claude Monet sets up his easel at the foot of a small hill. Up above, his wife Camille holds a green parasol, and their son Jean stands a little further off in the grass. The wind lifts her veil and the clouds race by. Monet paints in a few hours, with broad strokes, to keep the moment before it blows away. We seem to be looking up at them. The painting is in the National Gallery of Art, in Washington.

Vincent van Gogh loved his little bedroom in the Yellow House in Arles so much that he painted it three times. This is the second version, from 1889. He wrote to his brother Theo that the colours should rest the mind: lavender-blue walls, a yellow bed, a red blanket. Look at the floor, it tilts a little, as if the room were opening its arms to us. On the walls, Vincent hung his own paintings. This bedroom is in the Art Institute of Chicago.

May 1889. Vincent van Gogh has just arrived at the hospital in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. In his very first week, he goes out into the garden and paints these irises. He calls painting his lightning rod: it helps him feel better. Look at the leaves, like green swords, and that single white iris on the left among all the blue ones. The painting is now in the Getty Museum, in Los Angeles.

Arles, August 1888. Vincent van Gogh is waiting for a visit from his friend, the painter Paul Gauguin. To decorate his room, he paints sunflowers in a vase, almost entirely in yellows. He has to work fast, because the flowers wilt in a few days. Gauguin would love these paintings. Vincent signs on the vase, simply: Vincent. This version is in the National Gallery, in London.

Around 1831, in Japan. Katsushika Hokusai publishes his Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. In this one there is no wave and no people: only the mountain, turned red by the morning sun at the end of summer. The sky is blue, with rows of small white clouds. With barely three colours, Hokusai lets us feel the calm of a windless morning. These pictures were printed from carved wooden blocks, one for each colour.

Edo, the old name of Tokyo, 1857. Utagawa Hiroshige shows a sudden shower catching people on a big wooden bridge. The rain falls in fine straight lines, each one carved by hand. People hide under straw hats and umbrellas. Thirty years later, in Paris, Vincent van Gogh admired this print so much that he copied it in oil paint. Japan inspired many European painters.

Paris, 1877. Gustave Caillebotte paints a brand-new crossroads near the Gare Saint-Lazare. The tall buildings have just been built, and the cobblestones shine in the rain. People pass each other under their umbrellas, a little like in a photograph. Caillebotte was a painter but also a generous friend: he bought the Impressionists’ paintings to help them. This huge canvas is in the Art Institute of Chicago.

Winter 1565, in Flanders. Pieter Bruegel paints a series of pictures of the seasons. In this one, hunters come back to the village with their dogs, through the snow. Below, everyone is having fun on the frozen ponds: skating, playing, sliding. The black trees and the pale green sky make you feel cold just looking at them. The painting is in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, in Vienna.

Giuseppe Arcimboldo was painter to the emperors of Austria. He had a funny idea: to paint the four seasons as faces made of what each season gives us. Here is Summer. His cheek is a peach, his nose a cucumber, his teeth are peas, and his hair is made of fruit. He even wove his signature into the straw collar. The emperors loved these painted riddles.

United States, 1872. Winslow Homer paints a little red country schoolhouse in the middle of a meadow. It is playtime: boys hold hands and run in a line. The ones at the end are flung like the tip of a whip, and two have already fallen over! Homer loved painting children and simple country life. This painting is in the Metropolitan Museum, in New York.

string-array.name: story_texts
string-array.item: “I came into the studio through the back door, with empty hands and a lot of hope. The master handed me a brush: ‘Start with one area. Just one.’”
“I’ve already stained three aprons. The master laughs: ‘Paint on the floor is proof that someone worked.’ He showed me how to hold the brush closer to the bristles.”
“Today I ground my first colours. Ultramarine blue comes from a stone that crossed the sea. Now I know why we never waste a drop.”
“The master let me use his brushes for the first time. He looked at my canvas for a long while, then said: ‘Tomorrow, you’ll paint the sky.’ I didn’t sleep all night.”
“Visitors stopped in front of one of my canvases. They looked for my signature in the corner. The master smiled and said nothing.”
“This morning, a young boy pushed open the studio’s back door. I handed him a brush: ‘Start with one area. Just one.’”
“The master left me the keys to the studio. They say one last challenge remains: to paint every canvas at the highest level. The great masters call it a masterpiece.”
